title: Telemedicine and Triage
answer: Symptom routing, camera-based vital signs, wearables, conversational care and mental health signals.

children.name: Symptom Triage and Routing
children.blurb: Symptom triage and routing refers to automated systems that collect a patient's reported symptoms, estimate urgency, and direct them to appropriate care settings such as self-care, primary care, urgent care, or emergency services.

children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Camera-based vital sign measurement uses ordinary video, typically from a webcam or smartphone, to estimate pulse rate, respiratory rate, and sometimes blood oxygen saturation without contact.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care refers to physiological signals collected outside the clinic by consumer or medical-grade devices, such as heart rate, activity, sleep, blood oxygen, glucose, and single-lead electrocardiograms, and their use in remote monitoring, triage, and chronic disease management.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care in telemedicine and triage covers automated text or voice interfaces that ask patients about symptoms, history, and urgency before a clinician visit.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health refers to the measurable traces people leave through phones, wearables, telehealth visits, and online activity that may relate to mood, anxiety, sleep, cognition, or risk of self-harm.

sections.body: This field covers how artificial intelligence helps people get to the right kind of care without first seeing a clinician in person. Symptom triage and routing tools take a person's reported complaints and suggest whether they need emergency care, a routine appointment, or self care. Camera based vital signs estimate pulse, breathing rate, and sometimes blood pressure from a video of a person's face or hand. Wearable data in clinical care pulls heart rate, sleep, activity, and oxygen readings from consumer devices into medical decisions. Conversational care and its limits includes chatbots that ask follow up questions, and digital signals of mental health looks at typing patterns, voice, and phone use for possible signs of depression or anxiety.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Symptom triage tools are widely used by health systems and insurers, but they still make conservative referrals and can send people to emergency departments for problems a nurse would handle by phone. Camera vital signs work in controlled lighting and still faces, but accuracy drops with dark skin, movement, or low light, and few regulators have approved them for clinical decisions. Wearable data is useful for spotting atrial fibrillation and tracking sleep, but most consumer devices are not accurate enough for hospital monitoring and can create false alarms. Conversational care can handle simple intake questions, but it cannot reliably understand pain, nuance, or a patient who changes their story. Digital mental health signals are the least proven, with many studies showing weak links between phone use and a specific diagnosis. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, but a model existing is not the same as a model working in a clinic.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Start with Symptom Triage and Routing to see how a patient's words become a suggested level of care. Vital Signs from a Camera and Wearable Data in Clinical Care both cover measurement, but one uses a phone camera and the other uses devices on the body. A reader worried about accuracy should compare the camera page with the wearable page, because both claim to measure vital signs but with different sensors and error sources. Conversational Care and Its Limits explains what chatbots can and cannot do in a medical interview, and it is the bridge between triage and mental health. Digital Signals of Mental Health extends that idea to passive monitoring of behavior, but it should be read after the conversational page to understand the limits of inference from language and activity.
